title: Coils, Capacitors and Transformers in Lighting Equipment

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Training bench with a de-energized HID ballast kit, a contactor, a neon transformer, a 12 V landscape transformer and an LED sign power supply, covers off. Medium shot.
scenes.says: Almost every system in our Master Troubleshooting Guide has at least one coil, capacitor or transformer. Understanding what each one does explains the readings you'll take, and the hazards you'll face, including a charge that's still there after the power's off. Everything on this bench is de-energized.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-ups: the HID core and coil, then the contactor coil.
scenes.on_screen: Coil: limits AC current | ohms de-energized: low | OL = open winding | burnt varnish smell = failing
scenes.says: A coil is wire wound around an iron core. On AC, its changing magnetic field opposes changes in current, which limits current without much heat. You'll find coils in magnetic ballasts, contactors and relays. De-energized on ohms, a coil reads low, a few ohms to a few hundred. OL means a broken winding. A loud new buzz or a burnt varnish smell is a strong sign of failure.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up of the HID capacitor; trainer discharges it through a resistor tool, verifies 0 V, removes one lead and reads uF.
scenes.on_screen: Capacitor: discharge, verify 0 V | test on uF range, one lead off | compare to label tolerance (often +/-6%)
scenes.says: A capacitor stores charge, and it can hold a dangerous charge after power is removed. Bleed resistors fail. Always discharge through a resistor or insulated tool and verify zero volts before handling. Then test it de-energized on the microfarad range with one lead disconnected, and compare to the label tolerance. Bulged, split or leaking means replace.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.on_screen: Same uF, equal or higher voltage | never a different uF on an HID ballast
scenes.says: Replace with the same microfarads and an equal or higher voltage rating. Never substitute a different microfarad value on an HID ballast; it changes lamp wattage. Coils make current lag, capacitors make it lead, and designers pair them to improve power factor. When an HID capacitor fails open, the lamp may not start or may run dim.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Bench: a step-down transformer behind a clear guard; qualified trainer in PPE measures primary and then secondary; readings on screen.
scenes.on_screen: More secondary turns = step up | fewer = step down | 10:1 down = about 10x current
scenes.says: A transformer has a primary on the supply and a secondary on the load, sharing a core. More turns on the secondary steps voltage up, like a neon transformer. Fewer steps it down, like a 12 volt landscape transformer. Power in roughly equals power out, so stepping down ten to one raises available current about ten times. A small loose 12 volt connection can carry a lot of current and overheat.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: LED sign power supply on the bench: meter reads zero output with no load; load connected, output appears.
scenes.on_screen: Electronic supplies may read 0 V with no load | check secondary connections, test with load
scenes.says: Open-circuit voltage. With no load, a magnetic ballast or transformer secondary usually reads higher than under load. But many electronic supplies, like this LED sign supply, have a protective cut-out and show no output with no load, or a poor secondary connection. Watch: zero. Connect the load, and there it is. Before you condemn one, check the secondary connections and test with the load connected.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Graphic of troubleshooting logic over the bench.
scenes.on_screen: 1 Primary | 2 Secondary (with load for electronic) | 3 Primary good, no secondary: connections, fuses, transformer | 4 Both good: wiring and loads | Qualified persons only
scenes.says: Troubleshoot in order. Measure primary voltage; none means upstream. Measure secondary under the right conditions. Primary good, secondary missing: check secondary connections and fuses, then the transformer. Both good: the problem's in the wiring or loads beyond. Check live voltage only once your supervisor has deemed you qualified for this task, wearing the required PPE, with a CAT-rated meter verified live-dead-live.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Neon transformer close-up with a warning graphic; Matthew beside it.
scenes.on_screen: Neon secondaries exceed ordinary meter ratings: never probe with a DMM
scenes.says: Primary measurements on 120 to 480 volts and anything on a neon secondary are energized work: qualified persons only, PPE per our NFPA 70E program, and a meter rated for the voltage. Neon secondary voltages exceed ordinary meter ratings, so never probe them with a DMM. Lock out, verify, and discharge capacitors before you touch windings or terminals. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.
